source.title: Deep sparse autoencoders yield interpretable features too

record.tranche_reason: The post discusses superposition and interpretability, but its experiments score features learned by sparse autoencoders rather than measuring polysemanticity in the target network's neurons.
record.gate_note: The reported automated interpretability scores concern SAE features, not individual neurons in GPT2-small. They are recorded as a related but different construct, not as tests of the listed versions. The reconstruction-sparsity results and dead-feature discussion likewise do not measure neuron polysemanticity. Figure 3 values are not given numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The post trains deep vs shallow SAEs on GPT2-small layer-8 residual stream and scores SAE feature interpretability; it never measures polysemanticity of the target network's neurons, nor tests superposition as the cause of neuron polysemanticity. Its argument about superposition concerns why SAEs work, not why neurons are polysemantic.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the author finds deep SAE features on par with shallow SAE features in interpretability and argues this suggests superposition does not fully explain SAE success, while conceding a linear-superposition account remains possible and that dead-neuron differences confound comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates interpretability of SAE features with an automated scoring pipeline; it does not apply the original neuron-visualization or polysemanticity measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares detection and fuzzing scores and shallow versus deeper SAE architectures; the text reports slightly higher detection scores for both deep architectures and no lower interpretability scores for either on the tested measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Deep SAEs (1 or 2 non-sparse layers each side) give features scoring at least as high as shallow SAE features on detection and fuzzing auto-interp; slightly higher on detection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding non-sparse layers around an SAE's sparse layer does not reduce automated interpretability of its features.

record.problems: The author notes a large difference in dead-neuron counts across architectures, which may affect automated interpretability scores; total parameter count was not controlled. The plotted scores are not reported numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The post also reports reconstruction-sparsity and dead-feature results, but these do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the interpretability scores recorded here. No eligible numeric values for those results are stated in the text.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons measured in any language model.
Superposition discussed only as an explanation for SAE success; no test of neuron polysemanticity's cause.
Initialization, regularization or noise as causes not examined.
SAE depth varied, but no change in target-network neuron polysemanticity measured.
Auto-interp scoring used for SAE features; dependence of neuron polysemanticity on activation range or scoring not tested (only raised in a comment).

record.verdict_notes: Commenter luciaquirke notes features may 'sneak through polysemanticity at low activations', relevant to V7 but only as a suggestion, no data. Dead-feature confound and uncontrolled parameter count noted by the author.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier neurons or vision inputs are examined.
No transformer MLP neurons are tested for responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
The post discusses the superposition hypothesis as an explanation for SAE success, but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity pressure.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise are not tested as causes of polysemanticity in network neurons.
SAE depth is varied, but the study does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or a change in that share in the target network.
The study does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether their activations share a feature.
Automated interpretability uses detection and fuzzing scores, but the study does not test how neuron polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation scoring.
